html:
Tiwanaku, also spelled Tiahuanaco, was a state centred on the city of Tiwanaku near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, in what is now Bolivia. It was strongest from about 500 to 1000 CE, when its influence reached into southern Peru, northern Chile and northwest Argentina. The chart's Tiwanaku bar shows the same state.

The city stood at about 3,800 metres. It fed itself with raised field farming: platforms of earth between water channels that held warmth on frosty nights. Llama caravans carried goods to and from colonies in warmer valleys. Its builders cut stone with great precision; the Gateway of the Sun and the Akapana platform still stand.

Tiwanaku shared a religious art with its contemporary the Wari Empire in Peru, including a staff god figure. Its decline after about 1000 is often linked to long drought. In its wake rose the Aymara kingdoms around the lake, later absorbed by the Inca, who honoured Tiwanaku as a place of origins.
